messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Special Education Teacher
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 58

He is 35, a European man who has spent most of his adult life in classrooms designed for children who need steadiness, repetition, and patience. He works as a special education teacher, and before the robbery he thinks of himself as the calm one in any room. He is the teacher who notices when a child is getting overwhelmed before anyone else does, who lowers his voice instead of raising it, who can turn a bad morning around with a predictable routine and a joke delivered at just the right moment. He lives alone, is single, and keeps a quiet, orderly apartment not far from school. His life is not flashy, but it feels solid.

The robbery happens on a Tuesday in late autumn. He stays late at school finishing progress notes and preparing visual schedules for the next day. By the time he leaves, the streets are darker and emptier than he expects. He stops at a cash machine on the way home, thinking about a student who had finally made it through a full lesson without bolting from the room. He hears footsteps behind him but does not turn quickly enough. A man comes close, too close, and then there is a hand at his shoulder and something hard pressed into his side. The man demands his wallet and phone. At first he does not understand what is happening. Then he sees the man’s face—flat, intent, impatient—and hears the threat repeated in a low voice.

He remembers small details with painful clarity: the chemical smell on the man’s jacket, the flicker of the cash machine screen, how his own hands suddenly seem useless. He gives over his wallet, then fumbles with his phone. When he is too slow, the man shoves him hard enough that he stumbles and hits the side of the machine. He feels a burst of humiliation almost as strongly as fear. After the man runs off, he remains standing there for several seconds, stunned, then crouches to pick up the cards that have spilled from his wallet. His heart pounds so violently he thinks he might be ill. When the police arrive, he is already apologizing—to them, though he is not sure for what.

In the first days afterward, he tells himself he is lucky. He is not seriously injured. The bank cards can be canceled, the phone replaced. Colleagues say it could have been worse, and he agrees with them. He tries to return to work as if nothing significant has changed. But his body does not believe the reassuring story his mind keeps repeating. On his walk to school, every set of footsteps behind him makes his shoulders lock. He starts crossing streets to avoid men in hooded jackets. At night he replays the scene in fragments: the pressure in his side, the demand in the stranger’s voice, the instant in which the street becomes unsafe. Sleep turns thin and unreliable. Some nights he jolts awake convinced someone is in the flat. He checks the door lock more than once, then again.

At school he continues to do his job, but it takes more effort to appear composed. A sudden slam of a classroom door sends a pulse of panic through him before he can hide it. During fire drills he feels his chest tighten and his vision narrow. He is embarrassed by how quickly his body reacts, especially in front of teaching assistants who know him as unflappable. He becomes more irritable with small disruptions. When a student grabs unexpectedly at his sleeve one morning, he jerks back too sharply and sees the child’s face crumple in confusion. He is flooded with guilt. After that, he watches himself constantly, as if any lapse in control might expose something he cannot explain.

His world gradually shrinks. He stops staying late at school and leaves before dark whenever possible. He no longer uses the cash machine where the robbery happened and then begins avoiding that entire street. He declines invitations from colleagues to have a drink after work because it would mean walking home later. Friends notice he is harder to pin down, though when they ask if he is all right he says he is just tired. Being single, he has no one at home who sees how long he stands at the window scanning the street below before unlocking his own front door, or how he keeps the television on for company because silence makes him hear imagined movement in the hall.

What troubles him most is not only fear but a changed sense of himself. He had believed he could read people, stay calm, keep others safe. Now he thinks about how quickly that confidence vanished. He feels foolish for still being affected months later by what others describe as “just a mugging.” Yet the memory remains vivid and uninvited. Sometimes while helping a student practice emotional regulation, he hears himself saying, “You’re safe, take a breath,” and realizes he does not fully believe it for himself. He continues showing up each day, arranging schedules, soothing distressed children, and maintaining the structure they depend on. From the outside, his life still looks intact. Inside, he moves through it braced, watchful, and tired, as if the street has never quite given him back.
